messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun Mehta was 39 when his older sister died without warning. She had collapsed at home and was gone before the ambulance arrived. In the first stunned days after the call, what lodged in him most sharply was not only the fact of her death but the atmosphere around it: the funeral home, the smell of flowers, the sight of mourners speaking in hushed voices about who had been lost and who was left behind. He remembered standing near the casket feeling unreal, as if the scene were happening at a distance and directly inside his body at the same time. Since then, grief-related settings have carried a particular force for him. A funeral, a cemetery, even a conversation about someone losing a parent or sibling can pull him back toward that first week.

Over the months that followed, Arjun tried to get on with work and family life. He is an interior designer, and much of his day is spent meeting clients, visiting homes, and discussing personal spaces with people who often disclose intimate details about marriages, illnesses, aging parents, and deaths in the family. He has found that when a client casually mentions bereavement while explaining why they want to redo a bedroom or clear out a relative’s belongings, his stomach clenches before he has fully registered what was said. Around the anniversary of his sister’s death, this reaction intensifies. He starts tracking the date weeks in advance and becomes preoccupied with how bad it might be this year, running through images of himself falling apart at work, losing control in front of clients, or getting trapped in the same helpless shock he felt when she died.

Those moments do not stay as thoughts for long. When he passes a cemetery while driving to a job site or receives an invitation to a memorial service, he can suddenly feel as if the original loss is happening again. His chest tightens, his arms go cold, and for a moment he is back in the funeral home, braced for news that cannot be changed. He says his body “goes there” before his mind catches up. By the time he realizes he is only hearing someone talk about a death or seeing headstones from the road, he is already flooded and on edge. At home, his wife has noticed that after these episodes he is quick to snap over small things, especially if she asks what is wrong when he is trying to steady himself.

Because those reactions feel so immediate and uncontrollable, Arjun has built his life around trying to stay ahead of them. As the anniversary approaches, he becomes absorbed in mentally rehearsing the worst possible versions of the day, telling himself that if he imagines every way it could undo him, he will be less blindsided. He avoids putting the date on the calendar, declines family plans that might acknowledge it, and tries to keep himself busy with site visits and vendor calls so he does not have to sit with any reminder of his sister. He has also started steering away from grief-related events altogether. If he learns that a client meeting will include discussion of a recently deceased relative, he will try to shorten the visit or redirect the conversation back to fabrics, lighting, anything practical.

Yet these efforts have not given him the sense of control he wants. The more he rehearses catastrophe, the more vivid and near it feels, and the more watchful he becomes for signs that he is about to lose himself in it. Avoiding anniversaries has made the date feel more dangerous, not less; each year it seems to arrive with greater dread. Keeping away from funerals and other reminders has left him less able to tolerate the ordinary ways loss comes up in adult life, so even brief mention of someone else’s bereavement can set off the same jolt in his body. Afterward he grows irritable, ashamed of how harshly he has spoken, and even more determined to avoid anything that might trigger another episode.

What finally brought Arjun to treatment was a scene at work this past year. During a consultation, a client explained that she was renovating after her mother’s death. Before he could respond, he felt himself drop into that old sense that the loss was happening now; his heart pounded, his hands shook, and he had to excuse himself to the restroom. He later barked at an assistant who asked if he was all right. He came home frightened by how little control he seemed to have and admitted to his wife that he had been arranging his life around not being reminded of his sister. What frightens him most is that grief has become something ambush-like and dangerous, waiting in dates, conversations, and places he cannot fully avoid. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to remember his sister without feeling as though he is being thrown back into the moment of losing her.
